title: Inpainting for the Recovery of Low Dose EDS Datasets
content: EDS maps are formed using a focused electron beam which is scanned across the sample, with an EDS spectrum being acquired at each probe location. This data can then be processed to produce chemical composition maps, used to understand the structure of the sample. Early EDS was limited in its application, with Si(Li) detectors having relatively slow acquisition speeds. The application of silicon drift detectors (SDD), which were capable of operating at faster rates, enabled accurate analysis over much larger areas [1]. Due to its robustness and precision, EDS is a popular technique across a range of applications and industries, including biological and physical sciences [2]. In spite of these advances, EDS mapping is still largely time limited, with high dwell times typically needed at each probe location to acquire sufficient information, which in turn limits the scan size/resolution of the maps. Additionally, many materials are incapable of being imaged by EDS as these long dwell times, can damage the samples, rendering the results unreliable.
